messages.subject: Reporting main effects in glmer
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,


apologies for cross-posting but this is quite urgent and I haven't been 
getting a reply elsewhere.
Fairly simple question this time. I need to report a main effect and or 
pairwise comparisons for a model that has a binary DV 'Correct' and a 
categorical predictor X with three levels (A, B, and C).


The original call was:

 >object<-glmer(Correct~1+X+(1|Part)+(1|Item), family=binomial, data=data)


with the following summary output:

Generalized linear mixed model fit by maximum likelihood ['glmerMod']
  Family: binomial ( logit )
Formula: Correct ~ 1 + X + (1 | Part) + (1 | Item)
    Data: .....

       AIC       BIC    logLik  deviance
  218.9053  242.0455 -104.4526  208.9053

Random effects:
  Groups Name        Variance Std.Dev.
  Part   (Intercept) 9.0129   3.0021
  Item   (Intercept) 0.7356   0.8577
Number of obs: 756, groups: Part, 45; Item, 18

Fixed effects:
               Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept)     -95.14 4122464.75       0        1
A             89.88 4122464.75       0        1
B             90.75 4122464.75       0        1

Correlation of Fixed Effects:
      (Intr)   X
A -1.000
B -1.000  1.000

where Part and Item are random effects for participant and items. 
Basically the three groups are very similar in their response, where one 
group (the reference level group in this analysis) has no 0s and all 1s. 
Releveling generates a Pr(>|z|) of .54 for the difference between group 
B and C so I believe the model is ok.

In this scenario I would not expect X to have a main effect on the model 
but when I compare it to the same model minus the X predictor, R yields 
the following:


 > anova(object,objectminusX)

Data: data
Models:
objectminusX: Correct ~ 1 + (1 | Part) + (1 | Item)
object: Correct ~ 1 + X + (1 | Part) + (1 | Item)
              Df    AIC    BIC  logLik deviance  Chisq Chi Df Pr(>Chisq)
objectminusX  3 221.64 235.53 -107.82 215.64
object  5 218.91 242.04 -104.45   208.91 6.7367      2    0.03445 *

My questions are as follows:
1. Should this be interpreted as there being a main effect but no 
significant difference between the three levels of the predictor?
2. How do I report the result in my paper?

Many thanks in advance for any help.

-- 
Frank Romano

Sabanci University
website: http://sabanciuniv.academia.edu/FrancescoRomano

On Jan 29, 2014, at 10:17 AM, T. Florian Jaeger <tiflo-sMaJTQEtWn7RrdkEUGVx5Ydd74u8MsAO at public.gmane.org> wrote:

> I second/third both Martin's points about Baayen's book (which I really like, but it's not for beginners, unlike they are the type of person who sits down and learns a programming language) and Alex's enthusiasm about Gelman and Hill. It's a very accessible introduction to regression and multilevel modeling (through R, though not primarily). 
> 
> I think Shravan's new textbook is worth a look (http://www.amazon.com/The-Foundations-Statistics-Simulation-based-Approach/dp/3642163122). I worked with earlier versions and liked them -- provided you have an audience that wants to get an intuitive understanding of the underlying mathematical concepts, rather than primarily learning to apply models (I think both are fair goals, depending on your priorities). 
> 
> For some of the more complex concepts, Roger Levy has a collection of lecture notes (perhaps in press, Roger?) that I find very illuminating.

A belated follow-up…thank you!  The book not yet in press, but it’s closing in on being finished.  The complete draft-to-date can be found here:

  http://idiom.ucsd.edu/~rlevy/pmsl_textbook/text.html

R code for all the examples in the book is available on the webpage too.  I use this material to teach graduate-level probabilistic modeling for language, and others are welcome to teach from it as well. Those who are primarily interested in understanding mixed-effects models can benefit from going from the beginning through Chapter 8.  The book is set up to allow people to stop there, or to continue on to a wider variety of probabilistic models that are of interest in cognitive modeling of language.

I agree with previous posters that for a more extensive and dedicated treatment of mixed-effects regression in a very workbook-like and hands-on style (but also with sufficient background theory), Gelman & Hill 2007 is hard to beat.

Best

Roger

> In case it's useful, I also have a bunch of lecture slides on regression and mixed models created in knitr (with RStudio), i.e., where the code shown on the slides is the one that created the slides. There's further slides by Maureen Gillespie (on coding) and Dave Kleinschmidt (on plyr, data reshaping, and simulation-based approaches to e.g., Type I error analysis). Let me know. Happy to share.
> 
> Florian

>    Data: .....

>       AIC       BIC    logLik  deviance 
>  218.9053  242.0455 -104.4526  208.9053 
> 
> Random effects: 
>  Groups Name        Variance Std.Dev. 
>  Part   (Intercept) 9.0129   3.0021 
>  Item   (Intercept) 0.7356   0.8577 
> Number of obs: 756, groups: Part, 45; Item, 18 
> 
> Fixed effects: 
>               Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|) 
> (Intercept)     -95.14 4122464.75       0        1 
> A             89.88 4122464.75       0        1 
> B             90.75 4122464.75       0        1

> Correlation of Fixed Effects: 
>      (Intr)   X 
> A -1.000 
> B -1.000  1.000 
> 
> where Part and Item are random effects for participant and items. Basically the three groups are very similar in their response, where one group (the reference level group in this analysis) has no 0s and all 1s. Releveling generates a Pr(>|z|) of .54 for the difference between group B and C so I believe the model is ok. 

This is a well-known problem with the Wald z statistic: it goes crazy when the maximum-likelihood estimate of a parameter gets large (notice your ridiculous standard error).  This is a well-known issue with the Wald statistic; one of very many places that discusses it and will give you appropriate references is footnote 13 of Levy et al. 2012 (http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0010027711002010).

Keep in mind that when a variable is a perfect predictor (as is the case with your reference level), the MLE of the the parameter encoding the difference between that variable and other levels of the variable is actually infinity (or perhaps negative infinity).  You get a finite parameter estimate due only to the fact that glmer() is by necessity satisfied with an estimate that is “nearly indistinguishably as good as” the true MLE.



> 
> In this scenario I would not expect X to have a main effect on the model but when I compare it to the same model minus the X predictor, R yields the following: 
> 
> 
> > anova(object,objectminusX) 
> 
> Data: data 
> Models: 
> objectminusX: Correct ~ 1 + (1 | Part) + (1 | Item) 
> object: Correct ~ 1 + X + (1 | Part) + (1 | Item) 
>              Df    AIC    BIC  logLik deviance  Chisq Chi Df Pr(>Chisq) 
> objectminusX  3 221.64 235.53 -107.82 215.64 
> object  5 218.91 242.04 -104.45   208.91 6.7367      2    0.03445 * 
> 
> My questions are as follows: 
> 1. Should this be interpreted as there being a main effect but no significant difference between the three levels of the predictor? 

Your likelihood-ratio test is an omnibus test for an effect of X.

> 2. How do I report the result in my paper? 

Depends on what question you are trying to answer.  But certainly don’t use the Wald z score in this case.

Best

Roger

> 
> Many thanks in advance for any help.
> -- 
> Frank Romano

No it doesn't, it's the same result as you got with anova().  I'm not familiar with the lrtest() function, but I am concerned that you have some kind of serious basic misunderstanding if you think that this is different than your original result.

> So the lrtest works better here and I have no
> main effect for X but I am in dire need of suggestions

> differences between my predictors, if any exist.
> 
> So the question now is:

See above.

> As you pointed out Generalized linear mixed model fit by maximum likelihood
> ['glmerMod'] is outputting ridiculous St.Error amounts and indeed the problem
> seems to lie at the empirical level in the absence of incorrect responses for
> my C group (this seems to be comparable to the problem you had in your article
> in footnote 13 where I believe you had no NP answers).

In our work, we abandonded GLMMs because we couldn't get models with the appropriate random-effects structure to converge (though I should say that I might have handled this situation slightly differently today, with the benefit of hindsight from our research on Barr et al. 2013).  That's not your situation.  (While we're on that topic, are you sure that random-intercepts-only models are appropriate for what you're doing?)

> Should I no longer be running glmer on this type of data?

Once again, it depends on what hypothesis you're trying to test.  What I would definitely advise is that you don't use the Wald z statistic to assess significance for contrasts between two conditions where one condition is a (near-)perfect predictor of a categorical outcome.  But likelihood-ratio tests are still OK in this situation.  So I would make a couple of suggestions -- for simplicity, let's call your perfect-predictor condition A, and your other two conditions B and C.

1) To test for significant differences between A and B, throw out your C-condition data and use a likelihood-ratio test on nested models with and without the effect of X fit on the remaining data.  Similar for testing for significant differences between A and C.

2) To test for significant differences between B and C, either do as you did in (1), or choose either B or C as your reference level and fit a model on your full dataset.  In this case, the Wald Z statistic for the effect of A will be useless, but the Wald Z statistic for the difference between B and C will be fine.  Either approach should give you similar results (and I'd be concerned if it doesn't).

I hope this helps.  Let me say more generally that some of the confusion you're having suggests to me that you need to shore up your foundational knowledge of the theory and practice underlying these models.  GLMM regression is a pretty advanced technique, and you need to first master the basics, then master the more advanced technique. The questions you're asking are about the basics.  I'd strongly recommend you take a substantial amount of time to go through a good book such as Agresti's Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis, both carefully studying the theory parts of the book and going through the examples on your own.

Best,

Roger

messages.body_plain:
I've played with this a little bit for a data dive so I'm not an expert 
but here are some ideas:

rCharts (http://ramnathv.github.io/rCharts/) has interfaces to 
leaflet.js and d3, the former of which is a javascript mapping library 
(http://leafletjs.com/) and the latter of which is a javascript 
visualization library that includes mapping capability 
(http://d3js.org/, esp. 
http://synthesis.sbecker.net/articles/2012/07/18/learning-d3-part-7-choropleth-maps). 
I got the leaflet examples up and running quickly but modifying was 
tricky -- it seems targeted at someone who already knows both sides (R 
and leaflet/d3), and my javascript is very rusty.

The maps and mapextra packages have some map shape data but they didn't 
have the shape data I needed. I ended up googling and finding them 
through a US state or federal government website (can dig up the link 
but it only had US zipcode data, probably not what you want).

At the end what I ended up with was a combination of maptools and 
ggplot, largely based on this example: 
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/plotting-polygon-shapefiles. It 
involved loading map shape data into R, "fortifying" it with other data, 
and plotting it as polygons in ggplot2. This doesn't have the google 
maps back end that ggmap does, which was a desirable property in my case 
(can replot things without relying on access to google maps or the APIs 
staying consistent).

There's also a spatial CRAN task view with more ideas here: 
http://cran.r-project.org/web/views/Spatial.html

     Hope this helps!

             Mike.
